entries.sentence: The NHS describes colic as a baby crying a lot with no obvious cause, which it says usually gets better by around 3 or 4 months, with comfort methods to try.
entries.note: Colic is a baby crying a lot with no obvious cause; common; should get better by around 3 or 4 months.

entries.sentence: The NHS says colic is a common problem in which a baby cries a lot for no obvious reason.
entries.note: Colic is when a baby cries a lot with no obvious cause; common.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists clenched fists, a red face and drawn-up knees among the signs, with crying often worse in the afternoon and evening.
entries.note: Signs: hard to settle, clench fists, go red, draw knees up; more often afternoon and evening.

entries.sentence: The NHS says holding, winding, gentle rocking, a warm bath and white noise may help, and that there is no cure.
entries.note: Common suggestions listed; no actual cure, only relief.

entries.sentence: The NHS says anti-colic drops and herbal or probiotic supplements are not recommended because there is no evidence they help.
entries.note: Remedies such as anti-colic drops, herbal or probiotic supplements are not recommended; no evidence.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if parents are worried, and going to A&E or calling 999 for a weak or high-pitched cry.
entries.note: Call NHS 111 or see a GP if worried; A&E or 999 if weak or high-pitched cry.

entries.sentence: The NHS says colic is when a baby cries a lot and there is no obvious cause.
entries.note: Colic is when a baby cries a lot with no obvious cause.

entries.sentence: It describes colic as a common problem.
entries.note: Common problem.

entries.sentence: NHS Inform describes a baby with colic as healthy but crying often and excessively, and hard to soothe.
entries.note: Baby healthy but cries often and excessively and it is hard to soothe.

entries.sentence: The main NHS colic page describes crying for more than 3 hours a day, on 3 days a week, for at least a week.
entries.note: Main NHS page: more than 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for at least 1 week.

entries.sentence: An NHS Best Start page gives a pattern that has lasted 3 weeks or more, so the exact wording differs between pages.
entries.note: Best Start page says the pattern should have lasted 3 weeks or more; pages differ.

entries.sentence: Local NHS leaflets say crying in young babies typically peaks when a baby is around 4 to 8 weeks old.
entries.note: Crying typically peaks around 4 to 8 weeks (local NHS pages).

entries.sentence: The NHS says a baby with colic is often hard to settle.
entries.note: Crying is often hard to settle.

entries.sentence: A baby may clench their fists, go red in the face or draw their knees up.
entries.note: May clench fists, go red in the face, draw knees up.

entries.sentence: The NHS says crying may happen more often in the afternoon and evening.
entries.note: May cry more often in the afternoon and evening.

entries.sentence: The NHS says there is no known reason why some babies get colic.
entries.note: No known reasons why some babies get colic.

entries.sentence: Explanations it mentions include babies finding food harder to digest when they are very young, and food allergies such as cow's milk allergy.
entries.note: Some explanations: harder to digest food when really young; food allergies such as cow's milk allergy.

entries.sentence: NHS Inform says one possible cause is trapped wind causing stomach pain.
entries.note: One possible cause is bubbles of trapped wind causing stomach pain.

entries.sentence: The NHS says colic can affect babies whether they are breastfed or bottle fed.
entries.note: Colic can affect babies regardless of whether they are breast or bottle fed.

entries.sentence: These are possible explanations, not proven causes.
entries.note: Sources describe 'some explanations' and 'possible cause'; no known reasons.

entries.sentence: The NHS says there is no actual cure for colic, only ways to give relief and soothe a baby.
entries.note: No actual cure for baby colic, only methods to provide relief and soothe.

entries.sentence: Suggestions on its colic page include holding or cuddling the baby, gentle rocking, a warm bath and gentle white noise.
entries.note: Common suggestions: holding or cuddling, gentle rocking, warm bath, gentle white noise.

entries.sentence: It also suggests holding a baby upright during feeds so they swallow less air, and winding them after feeds.
entries.note: Sitting or holding baby upright during feeding to stop swallowing air; winding after feeds.

entries.sentence: For bottle feeding, the NHS says to keep the baby as upright as possible and make sure milk fills the teat so there are no air pockets.
entries.note: Sit baby as upright as possible; milk fills the teat, no air pockets.

entries.sentence: It adds that some parents use a fast-flow teat, which may help a baby swallow less air.
entries.note: Some parents use fast-flow teat which may help baby swallow less air.

entries.sentence: The NHS says an anti-colic bottle may be worth trying.
entries.note: An anti-colic bottle may be worth trying.

entries.sentence: A Frimley NHS page adds that if a baby finishes a feed in less than 20 minutes, the hole in the teat might be too large.
entries.note: Frimley NHS page: if baby feeds in less than 20 minutes, the hole in the teat might be too large.

entries.sentence: A Hampshire NHS page advises never forcing a baby to take the whole feed.
entries.note: Hampshire page advises never forcing your baby to take the whole feed.

entries.sentence: On breastfeeding, the NHS says a parent does not need to change their own diet as a first step.
entries.note: If breastfeeding, no need to make changes to diet as a first step.

entries.sentence: The NHS says remedies such as anti-colic drops, and herbal or probiotic supplements, are not recommended.
entries.note: Anti-colic drops, herbal or probiotic supplements not recommended.

entries.sentence: It states there is no evidence that they help colic.
entries.note: No evidence they help colic.

entries.sentence: NHS Dumfries and Galloway, citing NICE clinical knowledge summaries, says simeticone and lactase drops should not be recommended because the evidence is not enough.
entries.note: Says simeticone and lactase drops should NOT be recommended due to insufficient evidence, citing NICE CKS.

entries.sentence: Local NHS pathways differ on drops, and a Hampshire NHS page says there is no evidence that anti-colic milks bring extra benefit.
entries.note: Guidance on drops differs between local pathways; Hampshire page: no evidence anti-colic milks have additional benefit.

entries.sentence: MedlinePlus, a US source, mentions simethicone drops for gas and suggests asking a pharmacist or health visitor first.
entries.note: MedlinePlus mentions simethicone drops as option for gas; summary advised asking pharmacist or health visitor.

entries.sentence: The NHS says colic should get better by around 3 or 4 months of age.
entries.note: Should get better by around 3 or 4 months.

entries.sentence: Another NHS page says it usually stops on its own by around 6 months.
entries.note: Colic usually stops on its own by around 6 months.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if a parent is worried, if nothing seems to work, if coping is hard, or if the baby is not gaining weight as expected.
entries.note: Call NHS 111 or see a GP if worried, nothing works, hard to cope, not gaining weight.

entries.sentence: It gives the same route if symptoms continue after 4 months.
entries.note: Or symptoms continue after 4 months.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if a baby has a weak or high-pitched cry, or a cry that does not sound like their normal cry.
entries.note: A&E or 999 if weak or high-pitched cry or not their normal cry.

entries.sentence: MedlinePlus lists a sudden change in crying, fever, forceful vomiting, diarrhoea or bloody stools as reasons to contact a health provider right away.
entries.note: Contact provider right away for sudden change in crying pattern, fever, forceful vomiting, diarrhoea or bloody stools. US source; in the UK the NHS routes are NHS 111 or GP.

entries.sentence: Local NHS programmes say infant crying is normal, comforting methods can help, and it is fine to walk away for a few minutes.
entries.note: ICON message: infant crying is normal, comforting methods can help, OK to walk away.

entries.sentence: They say this is when a baby is safe and the parent needs to feel calmer.
entries.note: OK to walk away for a few minutes and return when calmer, as long as baby is safe first.

entries.sentence: They also say never to shake a baby, because shaking can cause brain damage.
entries.note: Never shake a baby; shaking can cause brain damage, fits, blindness, deafness, learning difficulties and death.

entries.sentence: If a parent feels they may shake or hurt their baby, the NHS says to get help straight away.
entries.note: If you feel you may shake or hurt your baby, get help right away.

entries.sentence: Cry-sis is a charity for parents with unsettled babies, and one NHS page lists its helpline as 0800 448 0737, open 9am to 10pm every day.
entries.note: Cry-sis helpline 0800 448 0737, 9am to 10pm 7 days a week; another NHS page gave a different number, so check Cry-sis.

entries.sentence: A GP or health visitor can also be asked for help.
entries.note: Textbook-level: health visitor mentioned by MedlinePlus; GP by NHS page for worries.
